query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor CaF2 phase (on the order of 1–3 wt%) directly into the high-entropy alloy (HEA) matrix will reduce both the friction coefficient and wear rate over a wide service-temperature range by enabling the in situ formation of a stable, lubricious CaF2-enriched tribofilm during sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: The untreated HEA exhibits standard friction and wear behavior without any self-lubricating tribofilm, showing elevated friction and wear under harsh conditions, especially at high temperatures.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a low-volume fraction (1–3 wt%) of CaF2 during alloy synthesis to ensure homogeneous dispersion within the HEA matrix.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted in ambient air under sliding wear (e.g., ball-on-disk configuration) across a broad temperature span from room temperature up to at least 600 °C, using typical service loads to simulate industrial moving components.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, in situ CaF2-rich tribofilm on the worn surface.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, the embedded CaF2 particles, benefiting from their layered crystal structure and intrinsically low shear strength, are selectively sheared to produce a thin, lubricious tribofilm that protects the underlying HEA. This film minimizes metal-to-metal contact and friction while sustaining its integrity over a wide range of temperatures, thereby reducing wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated HEA, the CaF2-doped alloy is expected to exhibit approximately a 30% reduction in the coefficient of friction and a wear rate reduction by roughly one order of magnitude under identical testing conditions.
generation.baseline: The tribological performance (COF and wear rate) of the pristine HEA without CaF2 addition under comparable load, temperature, and environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention may be less effective in environments that are extremely humid or chemically aggressive, where the stability of the CaF2 tribofilm could be compromised.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends the concept of in situ tribofilm formation—demonstrated in reactive systems such as Ag-doped and Mo-modified HEAs (as reported in PMC6164388 and PMC8448869) and tribocatalytic amorphous carbon layer formation (PMC12019924)—to a nonreactive, high-temperature stable solid lubricant (CaF2). However, its long-term stability, homogeneous dispersion in a ductile HEA, and resistance to cyclic loading are not yet established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set with 1–3 wt% CaF2 incorporated during synthesis and a control set without the additive. Subject both sets to identical ball-on-disk sliding wear tests across a temperature range from room temperature to 600 °C under the same loading conditions.
measurements: Surface characterization of wear tracks (using SEM, EDS, and Raman spectroscopy to detect and assess the continuity of the CaF2 tribofilm)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CaF2-doped samples do not demonstrate at least a ~30% reduction in COF and an order-of-magnitude decrease in wear rate compared to the control samples across the temperature range, or if the in situ tribofilm is discontinuous or degrades rapidly under cyclic load, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Intrigued by the extensive lubricious behavior of the HEA in ethanol, a further study has been conducted to analyze the capabilities of HEA nanoflakes in other solvents like water. The (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 powder is combined with distilled water at a concentration of 1.5g L−1. This water‐based lubricant solution was sonicated for thorough mixing (≈9 h sonication time) and spray coated uniformly onto the steel disk for ball‐on‐disk friction experiments across all loads from 1 N to 9 N. The results found all sliding tests to fail within short distances (Figure S5, Supporting Information). In Figure S5 (Supporting Information), the starting COF decreases with an increase in load, showing the intrinsic HEA behavior like in the case of HEA in ethanol. However, the HEA in water exhibits limited wear resistance and high wear rates in the magnitude of 10−6 mm3 (N∙m)−1 as compared to HEA in ethanol which has wear rates in the magnitude of 10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1. This shows that the ethanol solvent plays a significant role in increasing the tribological performance of HEA during friction tests. In this paper, the investigation on the tribological performance of PAO base oil mixed with Mg(ReO4)2 additive with four-ball experimental conditions and ball-on-disc sliding friction tests over a wide temperature range was implemented. In view of the test result analysis, the following conclusions can be drawn:(1)The Mg(ReO4)2 compound used as lubricating additive significantly improved the lubricating base oil in the condition of the four-ball test. The coefficient of friction and WSD were reduced by 30.8% and 28.5%, respectively, when the optimum concentration of 0.5 wt% Mg(ReO4)2 additive was dispersed.(2)The Mg(ReO4)2 compound could promote the antifriction property of the base oil at a relatively low temperature and possessed a superb lubrication function at high temperature conditions. The added Mg(ReO4)2 was deposited on the worn surface and generated a protective layer that improved the contact state of the rubbing interface. This layer formed at the elevated temperature range was mainly made up of Mg(ReO4)2 compound and some natural oxides from the metal matrix, while the appearance of the complex layer could effectively prevent direct contact between rubbing pairs.

In summary, we propose a strategy to design wear-resistant alloys through in-situ formation of strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surfaces during wear, a process which we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. A representative bcc structured (TiNbZr)75Ag25 (at.%) alloy was developed, which yields a two orders of magnitude lower wear rate than the reference TiNbZr alloy. Upon wear in ambient air, the (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy forms an in-situ 400-nm-thick amorphous-crystalline nanocomposite surface layer, through reaction with the environmental O, comprising an amorphous Ti17Nb13Zr13Fe2O55 matrix containing ~10-nm-sized Ag nanocrystals.
